He remained stubbornly silent, saying nothing throughout the journey except ‘that damned bug.’ I carried two lanterns with shutters, while Legrand took only the beetle. He had tied it to a short length of whipcord and swung it back and forth as he walked, rather like a magician. Seeing this final, unmistakable sign that my friend had lost his mind, I could barely hold back my tears. Still, I thought it best to go along with his wishes for the moment, until I could take stronger action with some hope of success. Meanwhile, I tried without success to find out the purpose of our expedition. Now that he had persuaded me to join him, he seemed unwilling to discuss anything he considered less important. Whatever I asked, his only answer was, ‘We shall see!’

We crossed the creek at the end of the island in a small boat, then climbed the high ground along the mainland shore and headed northwest. The countryside was extraordinarily wild and empty, with no sign of a human footprint anywhere. Legrand led us confidently, stopping only briefly now and then to check what seemed to be landmarks he had arranged on an earlier visit.

We travelled this way for about two hours. The sun was setting as we entered a place far more gloomy than any we had yet passed through. It was a stretch of level ground near the top of a hill that was almost impossible to climb. Thick woods covered the hill from foot to summit, broken by enormous rocks that seemed to rest loosely on the earth. Many appeared to be held back from crashing into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines cut through the landscape in several directions, making the scene even more grim and solemn.

The natural terrace we had climbed to was covered in dense brambles. We quickly realised that without the scythe we could never have forced our way through them. At his master’s direction, Jupiter began cutting a path toward the base of an immensely tall tulip tree. It stood on the level ground among eight or ten oaks, towering above them all. In the beauty of its leaves and shape, the great reach of its branches, and the overall grandeur of its appearance, it far surpassed those oaks and every other tree I had ever seen.

I know very little, and it worries me—just a little.”

“Tell me what is troubling you.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative, and an orphan like me. I love her dearly. She is five years younger than I am and lives with a farmer in the south. Poverty separated us. She knows nothing of what has happened to me, because I cannot write. Even if I could, how could I tell her? It is better this way.”

“Yes, yes. Better this way.”

“As we travelled here, I kept thinking something, and I am still thinking it now as I look at your kind, strong face, which gives me such courage. If the Republic really helps the poor, if they have more to eat and suffer less in every way, she may have a long life. She might even grow old.”

“And what then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think”—her patient eyes, which have endured so much without complaint, fill with tears, and her lips open a little further and begin to tremble—“that the wait will seem long to me, while I wait for her in the better world where I trust you and I will both find merciful shelter?”

“No, my child. There is no time there, and no suffering.”

“You give me so much comfort! I understand so little. Should I kiss you now? Has the time come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips, and he kisses hers. Solemnly, they bless one another. Her thin hand does not shake when he lets it go. Her patient face shows only a gentle, radiant courage. She goes ahead of him; then she is gone. The women with their knitting count twenty-two.

“The Lord says, I am the Resurrection and the Life. Whoever believes in me will live, even after death; and whoever lives and believes in me will never die.”

The murmur of countless voices, the many faces lifted upward, the pressure of footsteps at the edges of the crowd as it surges forward like a great swell of water—all of it vanishes in an instant. Twenty-three.

That night, people across the city said his face had been the most peaceful ever seen there. Many said, too, that he had looked noble and prophetic.

Not long before, a woman, one of the most remarkable people to die under that same blade, had asked at the foot of that scaffold for permission to write down the thoughts filling her mind. If he had spoken his own thoughts, and if they had foretold the future, they would have been these:

“I see Barsad and Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the Juryman, the Judge, and long lines of new oppressors who have risen by destroying the old ones, dying beneath this instrument of punishment before its present work comes to an end.

A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired escort went riding across Brockley meadows. While passing through a hedge, she tore her riding dress so badly that, on reaching home, she decided to use the back stairs to avoid being seen. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door happened to stand open, she thought she saw someone inside. Supposing it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her sewing there, she looked in to ask for help mending the dress. To her utter amazement, the figure was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat beside the window, watching the fading gold of the yellowing trees scatter through the air and red leaves whirl wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on one hand, and his whole posture expressed profound dejection. In fact, he looked so abandoned and so thoroughly worn out that little Virginia, whose first impulse was to flee and lock her bedroom door, felt sorry for him and decided to offer some comfort. Her steps were so light, and he was so deeply absorbed in his misery, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

‘I’m very sorry for you,’ she said. ‘But my brothers return to Eton tomorrow. After that, if you behave yourself, nobody will bother you.’

‘It is ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,’ he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to speak to him. ‘Completely ridiculous. I have to rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and wander about at night, if that is what you mean. It is the sole purpose of my existence.’

‘That is no purpose at all, and you know you have been very wicked. On our first day here, Mrs. Umney told us that you had murdered your wife.’

‘Yes, I freely admit that,’ the Ghost said irritably. ‘But it was strictly a family affair, and nobody else’s business.’

‘Killing anyone is very wrong,’ Virginia said. At times she displayed a sweet Puritan seriousness inherited from some distant New England ancestor.

‘Oh, I cannot stand the shallow harshness of abstract morality! My wife was extremely plain, never had my ruffs starched properly, and knew nothing about cooking. Once I shot a buck in Hogley Woods, a magnificent young stag, and do you know how she served it at dinner? Still, that hardly matters now; it is all over. And even if I did kill her, I don’t think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death.’
